## Purpose

This document synthesizes the main hypotheses tested in the FCFS clinic appointment simulation. The focus is on how class-specific properties affect access, utilization, delay, balking, and class advantage.

Each hypothesis is labelled as `Supported`, `Partially supported`, or `Not supported` based on the available simulation evidence. Sweeps are done with all other baseline assumptions fixed, with each step repeated across 100 seeds.

## H1 Evidence: Class 1 Cancellation Sweep {#h1-cancellation-evidence}

This sweep varies only Class 1's cancellation probability while holding Class 2 at the baseline cancellation probability of 0.10.

The hypothesis is supported if higher Class 1 cancellation probability lowers offered delay, lowers Class 1's own served rate, and leaves aggregate utilization flat or higher.

### Mean Offered Booking Delay

![Mean offered booking delay by class](../../../outputs/class1_cancellation/figures/mean_offered_delay_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether higher Class 1 cancellation probability shortens offered delay. All three lines overlap because cancellation does not differentiate offered booking between classes.

### Served Rate

![Served rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_cancellation/figures/percent_serviced_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether higher Class 1 cancellation probability lowers Class 1's own served rate. A cancellation may improve calendar flexibility while still harming the class whose appointments are being canceled.

### Average Utilization and Class Slot Shares

![Average utilization and class slot shares](../../../outputs/class1_cancellation/figures/average_utilization_aggregate.png)

This figure tests whether future cancellations are recycled into completed visits. If aggregate utilization stays flat or rises, then cancellations are not simply wasting capacity; they are reopening future slots that can be rebooked.

## H2 Evidence: Class 1 No-Show Sweep {#h2-no-show-evidence}

This sweep varies only Class 1's high-delay no-show probability while holding Class 2 at baseline.

The hypothesis is supported if higher Class 1 no-show probability reduces completed visits and utilization without producing a meaningful improvement in offered delay or balking behavior.

### Average Utilization and Class Slot Shares

![Average utilization and class slot shares](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/average_utilization_aggregate.png)

As Class 1's high no-show probability rises, Class 1 contributes fewer completed visits. Because no-show slots are not rebooked, those losses directly reduce completed slots which create parallel lines.

### Served Rate

![Served rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/percent_serviced_by_class.png)

This figure shows that higher no-show risk lowers Class 1's served rate.

### Mean Offered Booking Delay

![Mean offered booking delay by class](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/mean_offered_delay_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether higher no-show risk improves delay. A flat offered-delay curve supports the view that no-shows are mainly a completion loss rather than a congestion-relief mechanism.

### Balking Rate

![Balking rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/balking_rate_by_class.png)

This figure shows the no-show increase is not producing an offsetting benefit through fewer rejected offers.

### H2 Conclusion

H2 is supported if the no-show sweep shows lower utilization and lower Class 1 served rate, while offered delay and balking rate do not improve in a meaningful offsetting way.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)

## H3 Evidence: Class 1 Balking Step Sweep {#h3-balking-step-evidence}

This sweep varies only Class 1's high-delay balking probability while holding Class 2 at baseline.

The main hypothesis is supported if higher Class 1 balking probability lowers Class 1 accepted booking delay but also lowers Class 1 served rate.

The subhypothesis is that at low-to-moderate Class 1 balking probabilities, roughly 0.0 to 0.3, Class 2's accepted delay can rise because the additional appointment opportunities Class 2 gains are still farther out in the booking horizon.

### Mean Accepted Booking Delay

![Mean accepted booking delay by class](../../../outputs/class1_balking/figures/mean_accepted_delay_by_class.png)

It shows that as more long-delay Class 1 patients reject offers, the remaining accepted Class 1 appointments are more concentrated at shorter delays.

For Class 2, the initial rise in accepted delay is consistent with the subhypothesis. At low-to-moderate Class 1 balking probabilities, Class 2 gains access to slots that were previously unavailable, but those slots are still relatively far out in the schedule.

### Served Rate

![Served rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_balking/figures/percent_serviced_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether the lower accepted delay comes at the cost of lower access. Because Class 1's served rate falls as its balking probability rises, the decrease in accepted delay is not a pure improvement. It partly reflects selection: long-delay patients leave the system instead of being served.

### Mean Offered Booking Delay

![Mean offered booking delay by class](../../../outputs/class1_balking/figures/mean_offered_delay_by_class.png)

This figure supports the subhypothesis by showing the delay environment faced by patients who receive offers, including those who later balk. 

### H3 Conclusion

H3 is supported if Class 1 accepted delay decreases while Class 1 served rate also decreases. This pattern means higher balking can make the accepted-delay metric look better even while access worsens.

The subhypothesis is supported if Class 2's accepted delay rises at low-to-moderate Class 1 balking probabilities while offered delay remains high. This suggests that Class 2 initially gains access to additional slots, but those slots are still concentrated farther out in the booking horizon.

[Back to summary table](#summary-table)

## H4 Evidence: Balking Losses vs. No-Show Losses {#h4-balking-vs-no-show-evidence}


The hypothesis is supported if the Class 1 balking sweep shows relatively stable aggregate utilization despite declining Class 1 served rate, while the Class 1 no-show sweep shows declining aggregate utilization and declining Class 1 served rate.

### Balking Sweep: Average Utilization and Class Slot Shares

![Class 1 balking utilization](../../../outputs/class1_balking/figures/average_utilization_aggregate.png)

This figure tests whether utilization is preserved when losses occur through balking. Since balking happens before booking, rejected long-delay offers can be taken by other patients. Under the baseline's high-demand setting, this means aggregate utilization remains relatively stable as Class 1 gives up more appointment opportunities.

### Balking Sweep: Served Rate

![Class 1 balking served rate](../../../outputs/class1_balking/figures/percent_serviced_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether the affected class still loses access under higher balking. As Class 1's high-delay balking probability rises, Class 1's served rate falls. Aggregate utilization can remain stable while Class 1 access worsens, because Class 2 absorbs some of the released capacity.

### No-Show Sweep: Average Utilization and Class Slot Shares

![Class 1 no-show utilization](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/average_utilization_aggregate.png)

This figure tests the no-show side of the hypothesis. Because no-show slots are not rebooked, higher Class 1 no-show probability should reduce completed visits and lower aggregate utilization.

### No-Show Sweep: Served Rate

![Class 1 no-show served rate](../../../outputs/class1_no_show/figures/percent_serviced_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether no-show losses also reduce the affected class's served rate. As Class 1's high-delay no-show probability rises, more booked Class 1 appointments fail to become completed visits, lowering Class 1's served rate.

### H4 Conclusion

H4 is partially supported. The utilization portion is supported: losses through balking preserve aggregate utilization because rejected offers can be reallocated, while losses through no-shows reduce utilization because no-show slots are lost on the service day.

The served-rate portion requires qualification. In the balking sweep, Class 1's served rate falls as Class 1 balking rises, but the overall served rate stays nearly flat because Class 2 absorbs much of the released capacity. In the no-show sweep, Class 1's served rate falls and aggregate utilization also declines. Therefore, the hypothesis is supported for the affected class, but not for aggregate served rate under balking.

## H8 Evidence: Balking Threshold Crossing a High-Mass Delay Region {#h8-balking-threshold-evidence}

This hypothesis tests whether balking-threshold effects are smooth or nonlinear. The key idea is that threshold changes matter more when they cross delay regions where many patients are being offered or accepting appointments.

The hypothesis is partially supported. The evidence shows that threshold changes have stronger effects in the late part of the booking horizon, but it does not isolate `tau ≈ 11` as the unique point where the largest jump occurs.

### Baseline Accepted Booking Delay Distribution

![Baseline accepted booking delay distribution](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/accepted_delay_distribution_baseline.png)

This figure shows where accepted bookings are concentrated under the baseline balking threshold. The mass around later booking delays, including `tau ≈ 11`, suggests that threshold changes in this region can affect many patients.

However, this figure is only a baseline diagnostic. It does not show the accepted-delay distribution under every threshold value in the sweep. Once the balking threshold changes, Class 1 accepts and rejects different offers, which changes the future booking calendar and can shift the accepted-delay distribution.

### Accepted Booking Delay Distribution at Threshold 10

![Accepted booking delay distribution at threshold 10](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/accepted_delay_distribution_threshold10.png)

This figure checks whether the accepted-delay distribution remains the same after the Class 1 balking threshold changes. If the mass around `tau ≈ 11` changes, then the baseline histogram should not be treated as a fixed explanation for the threshold-sweep jumps.

This matters because the threshold sweep reruns the whole simulation at each threshold. It does not simply reclassify one fixed baseline group. Each threshold changes the booking calendar, which changes which delays later patients are offered and which delays appear in the accepted sample.

### Balking Rate

![Balking rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/balking_rate_by_class.png)

This figure tests the direct behavioral effect of the threshold change. Class 1's balking rate decreases as the threshold rises because fewer offered delays fall into the high-balking region.

The graph supports the claim that threshold effects are nonlinear in the late-horizon region. However, the largest change is not uniquely tied to crossing `tau ≈ 11`. This weakens the stronger version of the hypothesis that a single popular booking day mechanically produces the largest jump.

### Mean Accepted Booking Delay

![Mean accepted booking delay by class](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/mean_accepted_delay_by_class.png)

This figure shows how the accepted patient sample changes as the threshold rises. When Class 1 becomes willing to accept longer-delay offers, more long-delay patients remain in the accepted sample, raising Class 1's mean accepted booking delay.

The changes are consistent with nonlinear threshold behavior, but they do not show that the jump at `tau ≈ 11` is uniquely larger than nearby threshold changes.

### Served Rate

![Served rate by class](../../../outputs/class1_balking_threshold/figures/percent_serviced_by_class.png)

This figure tests whether the threshold effect reaches access outcomes, not only delay composition. As Class 1's threshold rises, Class 1 becomes more willing to accept long-delay appointments, which can increase its served rate and shift access away from Class 2.

The served-rate evidence supports the broader idea that threshold changes affect class outcomes, but it does not isolate `tau ≈ 11` as the only decisive crossing point.

### H8 Conclusion

H8 is partially supported. The evidence supports the broader claim that balking-threshold effects are nonlinear when the threshold moves through the late-horizon booking region. The accepted-delay histograms show that the system has substantial booking mass in this region, and the threshold-sweep graphs show nonlinear changes in balking rate, accepted delay, and served rate.

However, the evidence does not fully support the narrower claim that crossing `tau ≈ 11` specifically produces the largest jump. The baseline accepted-delay distribution changes when the threshold changes, and the largest metric changes may occur at nearby late-horizon thresholds. Therefore, the hypothesis is best interpreted as evidence of late-horizon nonlinear threshold effects, not as proof that `tau ≈ 11` is uniquely decisive.
